analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to make reasonable accommodations for pregnant workers instead of forcing them onto leave.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2017 with 27 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill was never taken up by the Senate committee it was sent to and died without a vote when Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act would have required employers to adjust jobs for workers with limits caused by pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions — for example, allowing extra bathroom breaks, a stool to sit on, or temporarily lifting a heavy-lifting requirement — unless the employer could show the change would be an undue hardship. It would also have barred employers from penalizing workers for asking for such accommodations and from forcing them to take paid or unpaid leave when a different accommodation would let them keep working. It died in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Pregnant workers and job applicants — particularly those in physically demanding jobs who today must choose between working under conditions that endanger their health, taking unpaid leave they cannot afford, or leaving their job. The bill would have let them keep working and earning while managing a pregnancy, with the same enforcement tools and damages available under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, and would have applied to federal, congressional, and state government employers as well as private ones.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must make reasonable accommodations to known limitations from pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions unless doing so imposes an undue hardship on the business [S2][S3].

Employers may not deny a job or opportunity because of the need to accommodate, may not force a worker onto leave when another accommodation would work, and may not retaliate against workers who request or use an accommodation [S2][S3].

The bill uses the enforcement powers, procedures, and remedies of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, including attorney's fees and damages, and strips states of 11th Amendment immunity from suits under the Act [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers — private businesses, government employers, and Congress's own employing offices — bear the cost of providing accommodations and would face lawsuits, damages, and attorney's fees when they fail to. Small businesses with tight margins would feel accommodation costs most, though the bill exempts accommodations that create an undue hardship.

drawbacks.text: Employers would bear new accommodation costs and legal exposure: the bill gives workers the same damages and fee-shifting remedies as Title VII civil-rights suits, which raises litigation risk for businesses, and small firms with thin margins would feel the cost of accommodations most even with the undue-hardship exception [S3].

The bill would open state governments to federal and state lawsuits by waiving 11th Amendment immunity, a constitutional change some states and officials have historically opposed on sovereignty grounds [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and the costs are bounded: an accommodation is usually something modest like a stool, a water bottle, or a temporary lifting restriction, and the employer can escape anything that would be an undue hardship. The main real cost is legal exposure and the expense of case-by-case determinations. For most employers this is a modest compliance burden; for pregnant workers facing unpaid leave or job loss it can be the difference between keeping income and health coverage during a pregnancy or not.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, so it died there when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 11, 2017 by Senator Casey, joined by Senator Heller and Senator Shaheen, and read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the same day [S3][S5].
The committee referral was the last action ever taken on the bill; it received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].
The bill had 27 cosponsors, including a Republican and two Independents, yet never advanced past committee [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have had to accommodate pregnant workers — and who could have been sued with damages and fee-shifting if they did not — are better off because the bill never moved. Pregnant workers in physically demanding jobs, who would have had a federal right to keep working with adjustments, gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — a Democrat (Casey) introduced it with a Republican (Heller) and 27 total cosponsors including 1 Republican and 2 Independents — but the committee that controlled its fate never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have required businesses to accommodate pregnant workers' limitations or face Title VII-style damages and fee-shifting suits. Its interest in avoiding those costs and lawsuits runs directly against the interest of pregnant workers in keeping their jobs and pay.

The bill would have covered state employees and waived states' 11th Amendment immunity, exposing state governments to suits for failing to accommodate. Their interest in sovereign immunity and avoiding liability ran against workers' ability to enforce the new right.

The bill applied its accommodation requirements to congressional employing offices and federal employees through the Congressional Accountability Act and related statutes, so lawmakers' own workplaces would have been bound by it.
